title: Host-guest Crystal Engineering Tailors the Room Temperature Spin Dynamics in Molecular Quantum Devices
authors: Ziqiu Huang, Angus Cowley-Semple, Irena Nevjestic, Yifan Yu, Mark Oxborrow, Sam L. Bayliss, Sarah K. Mann, Max Attwood
abstract: Molecular materials that enable coherent control over an electron's spin state at room temperature are promising candidates for quantum technologies, including quantum sensors and ultra-low noise microwave amplifiers, known as masers. Host-guest molecular crystals enable independent control of spin-active guests and their local environments to enhance molecular spin properties and so improve device performance. Using electron paramagnetic resonance and optically-detected magnetic resonance, we demonstrate the ability to tune triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation by modulating host-dependent lattice rigidity and vibrational coupling to significantly reduce the operating requirements for building useful masers. Importantly, the most rigid host, picene, reveals the ability to slow spin-lattice relaxation without lengthening triplet lifetime, though at the cost of strain-induced line width broadening and reduced triplet spin polarisation. We also find that deuteration reduces the triplet resonance line width and vibrationally-mediated triplet depopulation. Consequently, we find that perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl is the most viable candidate for building a continuous wave maser. This work demonstrates host-guest engineering as an important and practical method for tuning the spin-dependent performance of room-temperature molecular quantum technologies.
summary: The research demonstrates how molecular host-guest crystal engineering can precisely tailor room-temperature electron spin dynamics in pentacene-based quantum devices. By systematically comparing different hosts, the authors identify perdeuterated p-terphenyl as the optimal material for achieving low-loss, continuous wave maser operation. This work establishes a powerful design principle for molecular quantum technologies.
main_problem: The central goal is developing molecular materials capable of coherent control over electron spin states at room temperature for use in quantum technologies like masers.
main_result: Host-guest engineering, particularly using perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl (Pc-d14:PTP-d14), proves to be a highly effective and practical method for tuning spin dynamics toward building continuous wave masers.
method: The study employs advanced spectroscopic techniques including Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) and Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) at room temperature to probe spin relaxation, triplet population, and coherence times.
model_or_system: The physical system consists of pentacene molecules acting as spin-active guests embedded within various crystalline host matrices (e.g., PTP, NAP, PIC). The dynamics are analyzed using coupled rate equations describing singlet and triplet sublevel populations.
key_observables: Spin-lattice relaxation rates ($\omega_{ij}$), triplet population ratios ($P_x:P_y:P_z$), Rabi oscillation damping rates ($\Gamma$), fluorescence lifetimes ($	au_f$), and maser cooperativity ($\eta_{maser}$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, high guest concentrations ($\sim 10^{24} 	ext{ m}^{-3}$), and the influence of host lattice rigidity and vibrational coupling.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting time-domain signals to Bessel functions for Rabi oscillations and solving coupled rate equations for population dynamics; some rates are estimated based on literature or assumed equal across systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate photophysical processes, crystal structures, fitted Rabi oscillation curves showing field dependence, zero-field ODMR linewidths, and the setup/results for maser operation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for room-temperature spin control to characterizing various host-guest systems using optical and magnetic resonance techniques. It details how structural changes modulate ISC efficiency and relaxation pathways, culminating in a quantitative assessment of suitability for maser applications.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the challenge of realizing solid-state quantum emitters at ambient conditions by showing that crystal engineering offers precise control over spin Hamiltonian parameters (like zero-field splitting and hyperfine coupling) through host modification.
